The workflow begins by preparing single-cell data, typically in an [`AnnData`](https://github.com/bowang-lab/scgpt/scgpt/trainer.py#L9) object, for input into a pre-trained [`TransformerModel`](https://github.com/bowang-lab/scgpt/scgpt/model/model.py#L21). This involves loading the necessary model, its associated vocabulary ([`GeneVocab`](https://github.com/bowang-lab/scgpt/scgpt/tokenizer/gene_tokenizer.py#L24)), and configurations from a specified directory. The input [`AnnData`](https://github.com/bowang-lab/scgpt/scgpt/trainer.py#L9) object is then preprocessed to align its gene set with the model's vocabulary, ensuring that only genes recognized by the model are considered.

The process leverages two main functions: [`get_batch_cell_embeddings`](https://github.com/bowang-lab/scgpt/scgpt/tasks/cell_emb.py#L22) and [`embed_data`](https://github.com/bowang-lab/scgpt/scgpt/tasks/cell_emb.py#L148). The [`embed_data`](https://github.com/bowang-lab/scgpt/scgpt/tasks/cell_emb.py#L148) function acts as the orchestrator, handling model loading, vocabulary matching, and initial [`AnnData`](https://github.com/bowang-lab/scgpt/scgpt/trainer.py#L9) object preparation. It then calls [`get_batch_cell_embeddings`](https://github.com/bowang-lab/scgpt/scgpt/tasks/cell_emb.py#L22) to perform the actual embedding computation. This function efficiently processes cell data in batches, constructing a specialized [`Dataset`](https://github.com/bowang-lab/scgpt/scgpt/tasks/cell_emb.py#L64) and employing a [`DataLoader`](https://github.com/bowang-lab/scgpt/scgpt/trainer.py#L4) with a [`DataCollator`](https://github.com/bowang-lab/scgpt/scgpt/data_collator.py#L11) for batching and padding. The embeddings are extracted from the output corresponding to the special [`<cls>`](https://github.com/bowang-lab/scgpt/scgpt/trainer.py#L529) token, which represents the overall cell state, and are subsequently normalized. The result can either be a new [`AnnData`](https://github.com/bowang-lab/scgpt/scgpt/trainer.py#L9) object containing the embeddings or the modification of the input [`AnnData`](https://github.com/bowang-lab/scgpt/scgpt/trainer.py#L9) object with embeddings added to its [`obsm`](https://github.com/bowang-lab/scgpt/scgpt/trainer.py#L647) attribute. This modular approach allows for flexible integration into various analysis pipelines. For a broader understanding of how gene expression data is tokenized and managed within scGPT, refer to [Gene Tokenization and Vocabulary](#gene-tokenization-and-vocabulary).

### Gene Embedding Management and Analysis
The [`GeneEmbedding`](https://github.com/bowang-lab/scgpt/scgpt/tasks/grn.py#L18) class, located in [`/bowang-lab/scgpt/scgpt/tasks/grn.py`](https://github.com/bowang-lab/scgpt/scgpt/tasks/grn.py) and exposed through [`/bowang-lab/scgpt/scgpt/tasks/__init__.py`](https://github.com/bowang-lab/scgpt/scgpt/tasks/__init__.py), provides functionalities for managing, analyzing, and visualizing gene embeddings. Gene embeddings are numerical vector representations of genes, which allow for quantitative comparison and analysis of gene relationships.

The class can be initialized by mapping gene names to their corresponding embedding vectors, which are then stored internally. These embeddings can be loaded from files using a static method that parses a specified file format.

A key capability of [`GeneEmbedding`](https://github.com/bowang-lab/scgpt/scgpt/tasks/grn.py#L18) is its integration with [`scanpy`](https://github.com/bowang-lab/scgpt/README.md#L97) for comprehensive single-cell data analysis. It can convert gene embeddings into an [`AnnData`](https://github.com/bowang-lab/scgpt/scgpt/trainer.py#L9) object, enabling standard [`scanpy`](https://github.com/bowang-lab/scgpt/README.md#L97) workflows such as computing neighbors, performing Leiden clustering to identify gene groups or metagenes, and generating UMAP visualizations for dimensionality reduction. This allows for visual exploration of gene relationships in a lower-dimensional space.

Beyond basic management, the [`GeneEmbedding`](https://github.com/bowang-lab/scgpt/scgpt/tasks/grn.py#L18) class facilitates advanced analysis of gene similarities. It computes cosine similarity between gene embedding vectors to quantify their relatedness. This can be used to find genes most similar to a target gene or to construct a gene similarity network using [`networkx`](https://github.com/bowang-lab/scgpt/scgpt/tasks/grn.py#L7). The class also supports the generation of metagenes by clustering gene embeddings and provides methods to score these metagenes across different cell populations or conditions, which can then be visualized using clustered heatmaps. Furthermore, it can compute weighted or unweighted average embedding vectors for a list of genes, which can represent functional gene sets. The analysis and generation of cell embeddings are handled by related components. See [Cell Embedding Generation and Preprocessing](#embedding-generation-and-analysis-cell-embedding-generation-and-preprocessing) for more details.

## Example Workflows and Fine-tuning
The [`/bowang-lab/scgpt/examples`](https://github.com/bowang-lab/scgpt/examples) directory provides an illustrative workflow for fine-tuning an [`scGPT`](https://github.com/bowang-lab/scgpt/README.md#L1) model, primarily demonstrated by [`/bowang-lab/scgpt/examples/finetune_integration.py`](https://github.com/bowang-lab/scgpt/examples/finetune_integration.py). This script outlines the practical steps involved in adapting a pre-trained [`scGPT`](https://github.com/bowang-lab/scgpt/README.md#L1) model for specific single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) analysis tasks, focusing on learning cell embeddings and gene representations while mitigating batch effects.

The process begins with data preparation, involving the loading of scRNA-seq datasets and their subsequent preprocessing. This includes filtering genes, normalization, log-transformation, identification of highly variable genes, and binning expression values. Following preprocessing, the data undergoes tokenization, where gene expression values are converted into a format suitable for the transformer model by mapping gene names to numerical IDs.

The core of the fine-tuning workflow involves training the [`TransformerModel`](https://github.com/bowang-lab/scgpt/scgpt/model/model.py#L21) with a combination of objectives. This includes masked gene modeling (similar to Masked Language Modeling in natural language processing), which predicts masked gene expression values, and adversarial batch alignment. The latter, implemented via domain adversarial training, is crucial for correcting technical batch effects across different datasets or experimental conditions. This multi-objective approach allows the model to learn robust gene and cell representations that are less sensitive to variations introduced by experimental protocols.

Throughout the training and evaluation phases, comprehensive logging and visualization are integrated using tools like Weights & Biases ([`wandb`](https://github.com/bowang-lab/scgpt/README.md#L40)). This enables tracking of hyperparameters, monitoring various metrics such as masked mean squared error and masked relative error, and visualizing cell embeddings through UMAP plots. The evaluation extends to assessing biological conservation metrics using [`scib`](https://github.com/bowang-lab/scgpt/README.md#L99), which quantifies how well the model preserves biological variation while integrating different batches. This ensures that the fine-tuned model not only performs well on predictive tasks but also generates biologically meaningful representations.

### Fine-tuning an scGPT Model with Adversarial Batch Alignment
Fine-tuning an scGPT model involves adapting a pre-trained transformer model to specific single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) datasets, incorporating techniques such as masked gene modeling and adversarial batch alignment for improved performance and batch effect correction. The workflow is demonstrated in [`/bowang-lab/scgpt/examples/finetune_integration.py`](https://github.com/bowang-lab/scgpt/examples/finetune_integration.py).

The process begins with data preparation, where raw scRNA-seq data undergoes preprocessing steps including gene filtering, normalization, log-transformation, identification of highly variable genes, and expression value binning. This transforms the data into a format suitable for the [`scGPT`](https://github.com/bowang-lab/scgpt/README.md#L1) model. After preprocessing, gene expression data is tokenized, converting gene names into numerical IDs and padding sequences to uniform lengths, as described in [Gene Tokenization and Vocabulary](#gene-tokenization-and-vocabulary).

The [`scGPT`](https://github.com/bowang-lab/scgpt/README.md#L1) model, typically a [`TransformerModel`](https://github.com/bowang-lab/scgpt/scgpt/model/model.py#L21), is initialized with specific architectural parameters and can optionally load a pre-trained version. During training, the model uses multiple loss components. Masked gene modeling, analogous to Masked Language Modeling (MLM), involves predicting masked gene expression values, utilizing [`masked_mse_loss`](https://github.com/bowang-lab/scgpt/scgpt/loss.py#L5) and [`criterion_neg_log_bernoulli`](https://github.com/bowang-lab/scgpt/scgpt/loss.py#L16) for zero probability prediction. This helps the model learn gene relationships and context. Adversarial batch alignment employs [`criterion_dab`](https://github.com/bowang-lab/scgpt/examples/finetune_integration.py#L429) to mitigate batch effects, which are technical variations introduced during data collection. This involves a discriminator that tries to distinguish between different batches, while the model simultaneously tries to confuse the discriminator, thereby learning batch-invariant representations. This approach is further detailed in [Adversarial Domain Adaptation and Batch Effect Correction](#model-architectures-and-training-adversarial-domain-adaptation-and-batch-effect-correction).

Evaluation of the fine-tuned model includes assessing performance on a validation set using metrics such as [`masked_mse_loss`](https://github.com/bowang-lab/scgpt/scgpt/loss.py#L5) and [`masked_relative_error`](https://github.com/bowang-lab/scgpt/scgpt/loss.py#L28). Beyond these quantitative metrics, the [`eval_testdata`](https://github.com/bowang-lab/scgpt/scgpt/trainer.py#L589) function generates cell embeddings, which are then used to compute biological conservation metrics using [`scib`](https://github.com/bowang-lab/scgpt/README.md#L99) metrics and to visualize data with UMAP plots. These visualizations often illustrate how well the model has integrated different batches and preserved biological distinctions. This comprehensive evaluation ensures that the model not only accurately predicts gene expression but also generates biologically meaningful and batch-corrected cell representations. The utilities for evaluating these metrics are part of the general utilities for single-cell genomics workflows, as discussed in [Utility Functions and Diagnostics](#utility-functions-and-diagnostics). Experiment tracking and saving of models are managed through [`wandb`](https://github.com/bowang-lab/scgpt/README.md#L40) for reproducibility.

## Zero-Shot Applications and Tutorials
[`scGPT`](https://github.com/bowang-lab/scgpt/README.md#L1)'s zero-shot capabilities allow for the application of pretrained models to new datasets without requiring additional training, focusing on tasks such as reference mapping and data integration. These functionalities are explored within the tutorials provided in the [`/bowang-lab/scgpt/tutorials`](https://github.com/bowang-lab/scgpt/tutorials) directory.

A key component enabling efficient similarity search for zero-shot applications is the use of FAISS (Facebook AI Similarity Search) indices, which are managed through the [`FaissIndexBuilder`](https://github.com/bowang-lab/scgpt/tutorials/build_atlas_index_faiss.py#L28) class defined in [`/bowang-lab/scgpt/tutorials/build_atlas_index_faiss.py`](https://github.com/bowang-lab/scgpt/tutorials/build_atlas_index_faiss.py). This class facilitates the building, saving, and loading of FAISS indices from biological embedding data, which is crucial for quickly identifying similar cells or genes across diverse datasets. The builder supports various FAISS index types and can leverage GPU acceleration for faster processing. Embeddings and associated metadata are typically loaded from [`AnnData`](https://github.com/bowang-lab/scgpt/scgpt/trainer.py#L9) objects, allowing for integration with common single-cell analysis workflows.

The challenges associated with technical batch effects, which can arise from variations in experimental protocols, are addressed through continually pretrained models. The [`scGPT_CP`](https://github.com/bowang-lab/scgpt/tutorials/zero-shot/README.md#L18) model, for instance, is a continually pretrained version of [`scGPT`](https://github.com/bowang-lab/scgpt/README.md#L1) that has been supervised with cell type labels from the [`Tabula Sapiens`](https://github.com/bowang-lab/scgpt/data/cellxgene/metainfo.json#L52) dataset. This approach helps [`scGPT_CP`](https://github.com/bowang-lab/scgpt/tutorials/zero-shot/README.md#L18) to inherently account for cell types and technical batch effects, improving zero-shot performance and data integration across heterogeneous datasets. Further details on how [`scGPT_CP`](https://github.com/bowang-lab/scgpt/tutorials/zero-shot/README.md#L18) mitigates these effects are discussed in [Addressing Technical Batch Effects with Continual Pretraining](#zero-shot-applications-and-tutorials-addressing-technical-batch-effects-with-continual-pretraining). The design philosophy behind this is to maintain an unbiased, data-driven pre-training approach while allowing flexibility for fine-tuning based on specific analytical goals.

### Building and Managing FAISS Indices for Biological Embeddings
The [`scGPT`](https://github.com/bowang-lab/scgpt/README.md#L1) project employs FAISS (Facebook AI Similarity Search) indices to facilitate efficient similarity searches on biological embedding data. This capability is particularly useful for tasks such as reference mapping and data integration in zero-shot applications. The primary mechanism for managing these indices is the [`FaissIndexBuilder`](https://github.com/bowang-lab/scgpt/tutorials/build_atlas_index_faiss.py#L28) class, defined in [`/bowang-lab/scgpt/tutorials/build_atlas_index_faiss.py`](https://github.com/bowang-lab/scgpt/tutorials/build_atlas_index_faiss.py).

The [`FaissIndexBuilder`](https://github.com/bowang-lab/scgpt/tutorials/build_atlas_index_faiss.py#L28) streamlines the process of creating, configuring, and storing FAISS indices. It is designed to ingest embedding data and associated metadata, typically from [`AnnData`](https://github.com/bowang-lab/scgpt/scgpt/trainer.py#L9) objects, which are a standard format in single-cell genomics. When initialized, the builder takes parameters defining input and output directories, embedding and metadata keys, and critical FAISS index specifications. It supports the acceleration of index operations using GPUs and allows for flexible index types through the [`faiss.index_factory`](https://github.com/bowang-lab/scgpt/tutorials/build_atlas_index_faiss.py#L142) interface.

Data loading for index construction primarily involves reading [`.h5ad`](https://github.com/bowang-lab/scgpt/tutorials/build_atlas_index_faiss.py#L55) files, where both embeddings (e.g., cell embeddings derived from [`scGPT`](https://github.com/bowang-lab/scgpt/README.md#L1) models) and metadata are often co-located. After loading, the builder constructs the FAISS index, training it with the provided embeddings. A key optimization is the automatic adjustment of the [`nprobe`](https://github.com/bowang-lab/scgpt/tutorials/build_atlas_index_faiss.py#L145) parameter for [`faiss.IndexIVF`](https://github.com/bowang-lab/scgpt/tutorials/build_atlas_index_faiss.py#L229) indices, which helps balance search speed and accuracy. Once built, the index, its metadata, and configuration details are persisted to disk, allowing for later retrieval and use.

Beyond index creation, the system provides utilities for loading existing FAISS indices and their corresponding metadata. It also includes functions for post-processing search results, such as [`compute_category_proportion`](https://github.com/bowang-lab/scgpt/tutorials/build_atlas_index_faiss.py#L293) and [`weighted_vote`](https://github.com/bowang-lab/scgpt/tutorials/build_atlas_index_faiss.py#L308), which can be used to aggregate and interpret similarity queries, especially when dealing with multiple similar matches. This robust framework for FAISS index management is central to enabling rapid and scalable similarity-based analyses within [`scGPT`](https://github.com/bowang-lab/scgpt/README.md#L1)'s zero-shot capabilities. For more details on the practical applications, refer to [Zero-Shot Applications and Tutorials](#zero-shot-applications-and-tutorials).

### Addressing Technical Batch Effects with Continual Pretraining
The data-driven, self-supervised pre-training approach of [`scGPT`](https://github.com/bowang-lab/scgpt/README.md#L1) aims to reconstruct gene expression, which inherently avoids human bias in feature selection. However, this method does not explicitly mitigate technical variations, commonly referred to as batch effects. These batch effects can be categorized into two types: type I factors, which are global effects such as differences in cell capturing times and may be partially mitigated by pre-training, and type II factors, which are gene-specific influences like sequencing protocols. Type II factors can alter gene expression distributions and are often treated as important signals rather than noise by the pre-training process.

To address the challenges posed by technical batch effects and enhance zero-shot performance, especially when datasets exhibit observable technical variations, the [`scGPT_CP`](https://github.com/bowang-lab/scgpt/tutorials/zero-shot/README.md#L18) model was developed. This model is a continually pretrained version of the [`scGPT`](https://github.com/bowang-lab/scgpt/README.md#L1) whole-human model checkpoint, further supervised with cell type labels from the [`Tabula Sapiens`](https://github.com/bowang-lab/scgpt/data/cellxgene/metainfo.json#L52) dataset during its continual pre-training phase. By incorporating cell type information, [`scGPT_CP`](https://github.com/bowang-lab/scgpt/tutorials/zero-shot/README.md#L18) intrinsically considers both cell types and technical batch effects, leading to improved integration and a more unbiased data-driven pre-training outcome. The zero-shot capabilities, including reference mapping and data integration, are further detailed in [Zero-Shot Applications and Tutorials](#zero-shot-applications-and-tutorials) and demonstrated through tutorials within the [`/bowang-lab/scgpt/tutorials/zero-shot`](https://github.com/bowang-lab/scgpt/tutorials/zero-shot) directory. The documentation in [`/bowang-lab/scgpt/tutorials/zero-shot/README.md`](https://github.com/bowang-lab/scgpt/tutorials/zero-shot/README.md) provides further discussion on these challenges and how [`scGPT_CP`](https://github.com/bowang-lab/scgpt/tutorials/zero-shot/README.md#L18) offers a solution. This approach maintains flexibility for fine-tuning while providing a robust foundation for various analytical objectives.

## Utility Functions and Diagnostics
The [`scGPT`](https://github.com/bowang-lab/scgpt/README.md#L1) repository includes a suite of utility functions and diagnostic tools to support single-cell genomics workflows, covering aspects from environment setup and data processing to model evaluation and distributed training. These utilities are primarily located within the [`/bowang-lab/scgpt/scgpt/utils`](https://github.com/bowang-lab/scgpt/scgpt/utils) directory.

Core utilities facilitate reproducibility through functions that set random seeds for [`random`](https://github.com/bowang-lab/scgpt/scgpt/trainer.py#L49), [`numpy`](https://github.com/bowang-lab/scgpt/scgpt/trainer.py#L7), and [`torch`](https://github.com/bowang-lab/scgpt/README.md#L18), and manage logging to files. Functions such as [`get_free_gpu`](https://github.com/bowang-lab/scgpt/scgpt/utils/util.py#L76) assist in dynamically identifying available GPU resources. For data processing, there are mechanisms to convert categorical strings to integer IDs, map raw gene IDs to a predefined vocabulary, and efficiently manage [`AnnData`](https://github.com/bowang-lab/scgpt/scgpt/trainer.py#L9) object column names for consistency. Model-specific utilities include [`load_pretrained`](https://github.com/bowang-lab/scgpt/scgpt/utils/util.py#L309) for loading weights, which also handles parameter renaming to ensure compatibility across different model architectures or versions, particularly for optimized attention mechanisms. Evaluation metrics for single-cell integration are provided by [`eval_scib_metrics`](https://github.com/bowang-lab/scgpt/scgpt/utils/util.py#L394), which computes [`scib`](https://github.com/bowang-lab/scgpt/README.md#L99) metrics like [`silhouette_`](https://github.com/bowang-lab/scgpt/scgpt/utils/util.py#L409), [`graph_conn_`](https://github.com/bowang-lab/scgpt/scgpt/utils/util.py#L411), and [`nmi_`](https://github.com/bowang-lab/scgpt/scgpt/utils/util.py#L415), while [`compute_perturbation_metrics`](https://github.com/bowang-lab/scgpt/scgpt/utils/util.py#L452) calculates performance for perturbation predictions. For distributed training, decorators like [`main_process_only`](https://github.com/bowang-lab/scgpt/scgpt/utils/util.py#L622) ensure that specific functions run only on the main process.

A specialized set of tools for diagnosing and troubleshooting Flash-Attention usage within [`scGPT`](https://github.com/bowang-lab/scgpt/README.md#L1) is located in the [`/bowang-lab/scgpt/scripts`](https://github.com/bowang-lab/scgpt/scripts) directory. The [`diagnose_flash_attn.py`](https://github.com/bowang-lab/scgpt/scripts/README.md#L5) script helps verify which Flash-Attention backend (FA1, FA2, or standard PyTorch) is active, checks the eligibility of data types (e.g., [`fp16`](https://github.com/bowang-lab/scgpt/scripts/README.md#L9)/[`bf16`](https://github.com/bowang-lab/scgpt/scripts/README.md#L9)) for FA2 kernels, measures peak CUDA memory consumption, and validates checkpoint key mappings to ensure seamless model loading. This diagnostic script generates synthetic data and uses PyTorch's forward hooks to non-invasively inspect the behavior of [`FlashMHA`](https://github.com/bowang-lab/scgpt/scgpt/model/flash_attn_compat.py#L75) modules during a forward pass. It reports on environmental details, model configuration, and provides insights into potential issues like unexpected [`float32`](https://github.com/bowang-lab/scgpt/scripts/README.md#L59) inputs when Automatic Mixed Precision (AMP) is enabled. This helps optimize the computational efficiency of [`scGPT`](https://github.com/bowang-lab/scgpt/README.md#L1)'s transformer models by ensuring Flash-Attention is correctly configured and utilized.

### General Utilities for Single-Cell Genomics Workflows
The [`scGPT`](https://github.com/bowang-lab/scgpt/README.md#L1) repository includes a collection of general utility functions in [`/bowang-lab/scgpt/scgpt/utils/util.py`](https://github.com/bowang-lab/scgpt/scgpt/utils/util.py) designed to streamline various aspects of single-cell genomics workflows. These utilities cover environment setup, logging, data processing, visualization, model evaluation, and distributed training.

For environment setup, a [`set_seed`](https://github.com/bowang-lab/scgpt/scgpt/utils/util.py#L29) function is available to ensure reproducibility across random number generators in [`random`](https://github.com/bowang-lab/scgpt/scgpt/trainer.py#L49), [`numpy`](https://github.com/bowang-lab/scgpt/scgpt/trainer.py#L7), and [`torch`](https://github.com/bowang-lab/scgpt/README.md#L18). To facilitate debugging and record operational details, [`add_file_handler`](https://github.com/bowang-lab/scgpt/scgpt/utils/util.py#L40) allows logging messages to a specified file. The [`isnotebook`](https://github.com/bowang-lab/scgpt/scgpt/utils/util.py#L62) function detects if the execution environment is a Jupyter or IPython notebook, which can be useful for conditional behaviors like rendering plots. System utilities also include [`get_free_gpu`](https://github.com/bowang-lab/scgpt/scgpt/utils/util.py#L76) for identifying available GPUs based on memory usage, and functions like [`get_git_commit`](https://github.com/bowang-lab/scgpt/scgpt/utils/util.py#L102) and [`get_git_diff`](https://github.com/bowang-lab/scgpt/scgpt/utils/util.py#L106) to retrieve version control information.

In terms of data processing, utilities are provided for managing gene vocabularies and preparing data for model input. [`category_str2int`](https://github.com/bowang-lab/scgpt/scgpt/utils/util.py#L56) converts string categories into integer IDs, while [`find_required_colums`](https://github.com/bowang-lab/scgpt/scgpt/utils/util.py#L192) interactively identifies and persistently stores essential column names (e.g., cell type, gene name, batch key) for [`AnnData`](https://github.com/bowang-lab/scgpt/scgpt/trainer.py#L9) objects, saving configurations to JSON for future use. For handling tensor data, [`tensorlist2tensor`](https://github.com/bowang-lab/scgpt/scgpt/utils/util.py#L263) pads and converts lists of tensors into a single tensor, and [`map_raw_id_to_vocab_id`](https://github.com/bowang-lab/scgpt/scgpt/utils/util.py#L274) maps raw gene identifiers to vocabulary-specific IDs.

Model-related utilities include [`load_pretrained`](https://github.com/bowang-lab/scgpt/scgpt/utils/util.py#L309), which facilitates loading pretrained weights into a [`torch.nn.Module`](https://github.com/bowang-lab/scgpt/scgpt/utils/util.py#L310). This function incorporates logic to adapt to different attention implementations, such as Flash Attention, by renaming parameter keys to ensure compatibility.

For model evaluation, [`eval_scib_metrics`](https://github.com/bowang-lab/scgpt/scgpt/utils/util.py#L394) computes a suite of single-cell integration benchmark ([`scib`](https://github.com/bowang-lab/scgpt/README.md#L99)) metrics, including silhouette and graph connectivity, on [`AnnData`](https://github.com/bowang-lab/scgpt/scgpt/trainer.py#L9) latent embeddings. Additionally, [`compute_perturbation_metrics`](https://github.com/bowang-lab/scgpt/scgpt/utils/util.py#L452) calculates performance metrics for perturbation prediction models, such as Pearson correlations of gene expression changes, distinguishing between all genes and differentially expressed genes.

Finally, for distributed training, [`main_process_only`](https://github.com/bowang-lab/scgpt/scgpt/utils/util.py#L622) and [`MainProcessOnly`](https://github.com/bowang-lab/scgpt/scgpt/utils/util.py#L632) are provided to ensure that specific functions or methods run exclusively on the main process, preventing redundant operations in multi-GPU or multi-node setups.

### Flash-Attention Diagnostics and Troubleshooting
The [`scGPT`](https://github.com/bowang-lab/scgpt/README.md#L1) repository includes utilities to diagnose and troubleshoot Flash-Attention (FA) usage. These tools are designed to verify which attention path (FA1, FA2, or PyTorch) is active, check the data type eligibility for FA2 kernels, measure peak CUDA memory consumption, and validate checkpoint key mappings. This functionality is primarily encapsulated within the [`/bowang-lab/scgpt/scripts`](https://github.com/bowang-lab/scgpt/scripts) directory.

The diagnostic script, [`/bowang-lab/scgpt/scripts/diagnose_flash_attn.py`](https://github.com/bowang-lab/scgpt/scripts/diagnose_flash_attn.py), assesses the interaction between [`scGPT`](https://github.com/bowang-lab/scgpt/README.md#L1)'s [`FlashMHA`](https://github.com/bowang-lab/scgpt/scgpt/model/flash_attn_compat.py#L75) (Flash Multi-Head Attention) component and the [`flash-attn`](https://github.com/bowang-lab/scgpt/README.md#L18) library. It reports on the PyTorch, CUDA, and [`flash-attn`](https://github.com/bowang-lab/scgpt/README.md#L18) environment, including the detected [`flash_attn_backend`](https://github.com/bowang-lab/scgpt/scgpt/model/flash_attn_compat.py#L11). To perform its analysis, the script generates synthetic data and constructs a [`TransformerModel`](https://github.com/bowang-lab/scgpt/scgpt/model/model.py#L21), optionally loading a pre-trained checkpoint while handling parameter renaming rules necessary for [`FA1`](https://github.com/bowang-lab/scgpt/scripts/README.md#L8) to [`FA2`](https://github.com/bowang-lab/scgpt/scripts/README.md#L8) migration.

During a forward pass with this synthetic data, the script uses PyTorch's forward hooks to non-invasively inspect [`FlashMHA`](https://github.com/bowang-lab/scgpt/scgpt/model/flash_attn_compat.py#L75) modules. These hooks record critical runtime information, such as the [`FlashMHA`](https://github.com/bowang-lab/scgpt/scgpt/model/flash_attn_compat.py#L75) implementation type, whether [`use_flash_attn`](https://github.com/bowang-lab/scgpt/scgpt/utils/util.py#L333) is active, the input tensor's data type, and the status of [`autocast`](https://github.com/bowang-lab/scgpt/scgpt/trainer.py#L220) enablement. This allows the script to identify potential performance bottlenecks or instances where the system might be falling back to slower PyTorch attention paths. After execution, the script analyzes the collected data to flag issues like [`use_flash_attn=False`](https://github.com/bowang-lab/scgpt/scripts/diagnose_flash_attn.py#L221) when FA2 is expected or incorrect [`float32`](https://github.com/bowang-lab/scgpt/scripts/README.md#L59) inputs during automatic mixed precision (AMP) operation. The overall process provides a summary and recommendations for optimizing [`flash-attn`](https://github.com/bowang-lab/scgpt/README.md#L18) usage within [`scGPT`](https://github.com/bowang-lab/scgpt/README.md#L1). Further guidance on using and interpreting the output of this diagnostic tool is available in [`/bowang-lab/scgpt/scripts/README.md`](https://github.com/bowang-lab/scgpt/scripts/README.md).
